questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How politicians win elections in America
The history of advertising in New York
How opinion polls work and why they fail
Why so many young people don't vote
questions.why: They look into the polling industry after several well-known poll mistakes.

questions.q: What happened in the 2020 US election, according to Sam?
options: Polls said Trump would lose by much more
Polls predicted a clear win for Trump
Polls were completely accurate this time
No polls were carried out that year
questions.why: She says most polls predicted Trump would lose to Biden by a much larger amount than he actually did.

questions.q: What was George Gallup's simple idea?
options: To guess people's opinions from newspapers
To ask people directly what they thought
To pay people to vote
To study only farmers
questions.why: He wanted to know people's opinions and thought: 'why not try asking them?'

questions.q: What did the advertising agency Young and Rubicam hire Gallup to do?
options: Write speeches for political leaders
Make TV adverts for new cars
Sell toothpaste in shops across America
Find out if people liked products
questions.why: G Elliot Morris says they hired him to find out if people remembered or liked a certain product.

questions.q: Why does G Elliot Morris mention toothpaste?
options: To show Gallup moved from product research to politics
Because Gallup invented a new toothpaste
To show that politics is easier than advertising
Because toothpaste companies paid for political polls
questions.why: He says Gallup wondered, 'if it works for toothpaste, why not politics?'

questions.q: What is one reason pollsters failed to predict Trump's win in 2016?
options: They asked too many young voters
They only asked people online
They didn't ask enough white, non-college-educated voters
They asked the wrong questions about toothpaste
questions.why: Neil says they didn't ask enough white, non-college educated voters.

questions.q: What does G Elliot Morris think people should understand about polls?
options: They are always correct
They are less precise tools than people expect
They should be banned
They are only useful for advertising
questions.why: He says people should see polls as less precise tools that can't offer laser-like accuracy.

questions.q: What does Neil suggest might be the real problem?
options: Pollsters are dishonest
Voters lie to pollsters
There are too many polls
Our wish to know the future
questions.why: He says maybe it's not polls that are broken but our desire to know the future.
